title: Cheapest flights within k stops
problemStatement: LC 787. There are n cities connected by flights[i] = [fromi, toi, pricei]. Find the cheapest price from src to dst with at most k stops (≤ k + 1 edges). If impossible, return −1.
intuition: Constraint is on hops (stops), not just price. Standard Dijkstra settles by cheapest price and can discard a slightly costlier path that still has stop budget left — that path may be the only one that reaches dst within k. Stops increase by exactly +1 per flight, so process level-by-level with a FIFO queue (no PQ). Bellman-Ford with at most k+1 relaxations is the cleanest optimal.

approaches.title: Trap: standard Dijkstra (fails)
approaches.idea: Run classic Dijkstra on prices only (min-heap by cost, settle a city when first popped). Wrong under a stop limit: a cheap path that burns many stops can “win” and block a pricier path with fewer stops that still fits in k.
approaches.time: O((n+m) log n) if it were correct
approaches.whyWorks: It doesn’t. Dijkstra assumes once a node is settled at minimum cost, that label is final. With ≤ k stops, “minimum cost so far” is not enough — state is (node, stops_used). A first-pop settle can freeze a cheap/many-stops label and never explore a dearer/few-stops continuation that alone reaches dst in budget.

approaches.title: Better: BFS by stops (no PQ)
approaches.idea: Each flight adds exactly one stop. Queue states (city, stop_count, price). Skip when stop_count == k+1. Relax neighbor if cheaper price; FIFO order = increasing stops, so no priority queue and no log factor.
algorithm: While queue: pop (u, stops, price); if stops == k+1 → continue
For each flight u→v with cost dp: np = price + dp; if np < price_taken[v] → update and enqueue (v, stops+1, np)
approaches.time: O(n · k) worst-case expansions bounded by stops (practically O(m · k))
approaches.whyWorks: Stops are the constrained resource and grow by +1 every edge — BFS layers = stop layers. FIFO already expands in the order that makes the price_taken pruning safe: fewer-stop paths are processed before more-stop ones, so a dearer path never blocks a cheaper later path incorrectly the way Dijkstra’s price-first settle does. No heap ⇒ no log overhead.
approaches.dryRun:
k=0, flights 0→1:100, 0→2:500, 1→2:100, src=0,dst=2:
queue starts (0,0,0) → enqueue (1,1,100), (2,1,500); price_taken[2]=500
stop_count==1==k+1 → no further edges from 1 or 2 → answer 500

approaches.title: Optimal: Bellman-Ford (≤ k+1 relaxations)
approaches.idea: Cheapest path with at most k stops = shortest path using at most k+1 edges. Run Bellman-Ford for exactly k+1 rounds; each round allows one more edge. Copy dist before each round so updates use only the previous hop count.
algorithm: for each flight u→v with cost w: if dist[u] + w < temp[v] → temp[v] = dist[u] + w
approaches.whyWorks: After t relax rounds, dist[v] is the cheapest way to v using ≤ t edges. Cap rounds at k+1 (= at most k stops). The temp array prevents using an edge twice in the same round (same hop count).
approaches.dryRun: k=1 → 2 rounds. Round 1: only direct edges from src. Round 2: one-stop paths. Matches BFS layers.

python.notes: Optimal: Bellman-Ford capped at k+1 edge relaxations. Prefer this in interviews as the cleanest O(m·k) solution.

java.notes: Same k+1 Bellman-Ford rounds; clone before each round.

specialTechnique.title: Why standard Dijkstra fails, but stop-BFS works (no PQ)
specialTechnique.body:
State is (city, stops), not city alone.

Standard Dijkstra (price-first settle):
• Settles a city at the globally cheapest price seen so far.
• That path may have used many stops.
• A slightly costlier path with fewer stops is never expanded — yet it may be the only one that still reaches dst within k.
• Fixing Dijkstra needs an explicit stops dimension (and careful settling); a plain PQ on price is not enough.

Why normal BFS / FIFO works without a PQ:
• Every flight increases stop_count by exactly +1 (uniform hop growth).
• FIFO ⇒ process in increasing stops — same role a PQ plays for distance in Dijkstra.
• You are shortest-path-ing on the stop metric (unit per edge), while price is only the value you minimize with a dist array.
• No heap ⇒ avoid O(log) overhead; complexity is driven by O(m·k) style expansions.

Bellman-Ford (optimal here):
• At most k stops ⇒ at most k+1 edges ⇒ exactly k+1 relax rounds.
• Cleanest statement of the constraint; preferred optimal.

edgeCases: Cheaper path uses too many stops; dearer path fits in k
commonMistakes: Plain Dijkstra on price only (ignores / mishandles k)
Relaxing in place in Bellman-Ford without a temp copy (uses > t edges in one round)
Off-by-one: k stops ⇒ k+1 edges / k+1 BFS layers
Using a PQ “because weighted” when the ordered dimension is stops (+1), not price
patternRecognition: Cheapest / shortest with at most K edges or K stops
followUps: What if edges can be negative? (Bellman-Ford still fine; Dijkstra still wrong)
At most k cost instead of k stops?
interviewInsight: Say: “Standard Dijkstra fails because settling by price ignores remaining stop budget. Stops grow by +1 ⇒ BFS/queue, no PQ. Optimal: Bellman-Ford for k+1 rounds.”
